abstract: The effects of beauty on judgment and behavior are well-established and somewhat "unidirectional" (i.e., it seems that only beautiful people reap social benefits). In particular, a person's beauty does not seem to have any effect on his/her own prosocial behavior. In the current research, we focus on how people relate themselves to beauty, namely beauty mindset, and how it may shape prosocial and altruistic behavior. We present 10 experiments (N = 4,449). Participants who hold a beauty growth-mindset (i.e., believing that beauty is improvable) donated more money to charity (vs. fixed-mindset), were more likely to get vaccinated against COVID-19 after exposure to an intervention focusing on herd-protection (vs. self-protection), and showed increased intention to engage in other forms of prosocial and altruistic behavior. Empirically, these effects are mediated by a self-perception of the ability to exert impact on others. The present research serves as a starting point for investigating how beauty growth-mindset brings profound societal effects such as promoting prosociality.

abstract: Background Long-segment colonic Hirschsprung disease (LScHD) presents significant technical challenges during definitive pull-through surgery because of limited bowel length, difficult mesenteric orientation, and variable vascular anatomy. Adjunctive maneuver such as the Turnbull and Deloyer's procedures are described, but they are technically demanding. We are sharing our experience with an alternative maneuver, i.e., the Limited Ladd's procedure (LLP). LLP involves straightening the duodenum, mobilising the duodenojejunal flexure, and then placing the bowel in a non-rotational configuration, with the small intestine on the right and the colon on the left. We evaluated the safety, feasibility, and short-term outcomes of incorporating LLP during Duhamel pull-through (DPT) for LScHD. Methods A retrospective descriptive study was conducted on LScHD managed between 2014 and 2024. All children underwent a standardized two-stage approach: initial diversion followed by definitive DPT with LLP. Demographic data, disease extent, operative findings, postoperative recovery, complications, and short-term follow-up outcomes were analyzed. Results Twenty-three children with LScHD underwent DPT with LLP. The pull-through segment involved the transverse colon (n=7), ascending colon (n=6), descending colon (n=5), splenic flexure (n=3), and hepatic flexure (n=2). Three children required an additional right upper quadrant incision to facilitate duodenal mobilization. The mean operative time was 170 minutes, and the blood loss was 60 mL. Postoperatively, the feeding was started on day 7 (mean), and the mean hospital stay was 8 days. No intraoperative or immediate postoperative complications (stricture, bowel ischemia, or internal herniation) related to LLP were recorded. Conclusion Although this is a retrospective study with a limited sample size, an analysis of the short term results indicate that the LLP is a safe and feasible adjunct during DPT for LScHD when conventional mobilization is insufficient.

abstract: Exercise testing is an established tool for assessing cardiorespiratory function, guiding management, and predicting outcomes in children, adolescents, and adults with congenital and/or paediatric acquired heart disease. Despite its widespread use, substantial variability exists among clinical paediatric exercise laboratories in testing protocols, calibration techniques, data interpretation, and reporting, limiting multicentre collaboration and data comparability. To describe the formation of a registry focused on pediatric exercise testing. The Pediatric Exercise Data Analytics and Learning Network was established in 2023 by six institutions as the first multicentre paediatric-focused exercise testing registry in the United States dedicated to patients with heart disease. The Pediatric Exercise Data Analytics and Learning Network has two primary actions: 1) develop and maintain a multicentre registry with uniform data definitions to support quality improvement and research; and 2) establish a learning network to advance education and knowledge sharing through standard operating procedures, benchmarking dashboards, and collaborative initiatives. Integration with Cardiac Networks United links the Pediatric Exercise Data Analytics and Learning Network's functional exercise testing data with existing longitudinal heart disease registries, creating opportunities for high-impact quality improvement and research. To foster objectives, the Pediatric Exercise Data Analytics and Learning Network aims to build a diverse network of both individual and hospital members who will work collaboratively to improve the consistency and value of paediatric and congenital exercise testing, advance quality improvement and research, and enhance long-term outcomes for patients with heart disease. This document describes the formation of PEDAL including organizational structure, database creation, and future directions.

abstract: For nearly fifty years, federal corporate food waste legislation has consistently employed an aretaic (virtue-based) theoretical framework that assumes corporations will act as “Good Samaritans” when provided with appropriate incentives and liability protections. Beginning with Federal Tax Code Section 170(e)(3) in 1976 and continuing through the Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act (1996), the Federal Food Donation Act (2008), the Agri-cultural Improvement Act (2018), and the Food Donation Improvement Act (2022), United States policy has relied exclusively on voluntary compliance mechanisms rather than mandatory regulations. This Article argues that this approach is built on a myth, and that the myth operates on three interlocking levels. At the legislative level, it holds that corporations will donate surplus food if liability barriers are removed, a claim that fifty years of evidence has consistently refuted. At the hermeneutic level, it misreads the parable of the Good Samaritan itself: corporations in the food waste context are not the Samaritan, who acted voluntarily out of genuine compassion, but the innkeeper, who provided services in exchange for guaranteed payment. At the ideological level, it assumes that virtue can be cultivated in profit-driven entities whose fiduciary obligations run not to hungry communities but to shareholders. The consequences of this myth are measurable. Despite decades of tax incentives and liability shields, corporate food waste has increased from 30% of the available food supply in 1974 to nearly 40% today, while 47.4 million Americans experience food insecurity. Food waste in United States landfills generates 34% of all human-related methane emissions, substantially con-tributing to climate change that disproportionately harms the communities that food donation policies were designed to serve. The persistence of incidents like the 2021 Portland Fred Meyer controversy—where thousands of pounds of edible food were discarded and guarded from recovery by residents during a community crisis—demonstrates that voluntary approaches fail precisely when they are needed most. Even industry leaders fall short: after nine years of its Zero Hunger | Zero Waste initiative, Kroger, ranked first among United States supermarket chains for food waste commitment by the Center for Biological Diversity in 2019, only achieved a cumulative food waste reduction of less than 4% against a stated goal of 50% by 2025. This Article provides a comprehensive theoretical analysis of United States corporate food waste legislation, examining why virtue-based approaches have systematically failed to address the interconnected crises of food waste, food insecurity, and environmental harm. The analysis demonstrates that aretaic theory, which seeks to cultivate virtue through indirect encouragement rather than direct mandates, is fundamentally incompatible with corporate shareholder theory and profit-maximization imperatives. The Article further critiques France’s Garot Law, which mandates supermarket food donations through categorical duties, demonstrating that while this deontological approach achieved impressive increases in food donations, it failed to meaningfully reduce overall food insecurity due to its rigid, context-insensitive framework and the absence of monitoring capacity sufficient to ensure that donated food reached food-insecure communities. Moving beyond these existing approaches, this Article proposes a consequentialist-based Corporate Partner Food Waste Act, grounded in Congress’ Commerce Clause authority and administered by the EPA. Rather than assuming corporations will choose to do good, the Act would ensure they do good as a natural consequence of pursuing their interests within a well-designed system of mandatory requirements and measurable outcomes. The framework establishes food recovery requirements differentiated by geographic proximity to food-insecure communities—using USDA Food Access Research Atlas definitions as the baseline—creating “Priority Zones” and “Standard Zones” with distinct obligations tied to community need. Penalties are anchored to company revenue rather than fixed amounts, ensuring that the cost of non-compliance consistently exceeds the cost of compliance regardless of a company’s size. Annual performance reviews, comprehensive data collection, and an EPA Food Waste Reduction Coordinator provide the monitoring infrastructure that voluntary frameworks have consistently lacked. After five decades of legislative failure, this Article argues that the path forward requires abandoning the Good Samaritan myth entirely and replacing it with a regulatory framework that treats corporations not as potential virtuous actors, but as corporate partners whose obligations are enforceable, measurable, and calibrated to actual outcomes.

abstract: Introduction Since teachers play a pivotal role in students' well-being and school engagement, expecting to be rejected by a teacher based on a persons' background could have negative effects on affective and cognitive academic outcomes. This paper explores the hitherto understudied construct of students' background-based rejection expectation by teachers and school engagement. Method In a study with 7th grade students in Germany, we addressed the question of whether students' expectation of rejection by teachers is connected to their school engagement, grades, self-esteem, and academic self-concept. We explored which groups of students expect to be rejected, and we checked whether strong emotional teacher support can moderate the effect of rejection expectation on school engagement. Results A strong expectation of rejection is associated with lower emotional and behavioral school engagement, lower grades, self-esteem, and academic self-concept. Ethnic minority students and students with lower cultural capital expect rejection more than their peers. There is indication that a strong emotional teacher support could moderate the relationship between rejection expectation and minority students' emotional and cognitive school engagement. Discussion Expectation of rejection can be associated with several negative academic outcomes. More research is needed to better understand when and how students expect rejection. It is relevant to understand how schools can be culturally responsive and inclusive.

abstract: The paper proposes the Truth-Default Ingroup Hypothesis (TDIH), an evolutionary framework linking moral psychology, cumulative cultural learning, and online social polarization.Grounded in long-term empirical research on online public opinion and social data analysis, and drawing on evolutionary anthropology and theories of cumulative cultural learning, I examine how human moral emotions-originally evolved to promote cooperation and suppress deception-shape contemporary forms of online behavior such as flaming, outrage, misinformation, and social polarization.Building on this framework, I propose a novel theoretical model: the Truth-Default Ingroup Hypothesis (TDIH).This hypothesis argues that humans domesticated the deceptive potential of language by forming "truth-default ingroups" sustained by norms, reputation, and sanctions.These trust-based communities enabled cumulative learning but also fostered ingroup favoritism and parochial altruism.In digital society, the same evolved moral mechanisms-truth bias, conformity, and third-party punishment-are amplified by social media, producing moral outrage, polarization, and misinformation.Online flaming, hate speech, and "cancel culture" thus represent technologically intensified expressions of evolutionary cooperative instincts.Recognizing these evolutionary underpinnings allows sociology to reframe digital moral conflict not as a technological anomaly, but as an extension of humanity's deep moral architecture.

abstract: BACKGROUND: The experimental evaluation of young children's socio-emotional abilities is limited by the lack of existing specific measures to assess this population and by the relative difficulty for researchers to adapt measures designed for the general population. METHODS: This study examined six early social-emotional abilities in 86 typically developing children aged 1 to 3 years using an eye-tracking-based experimental paradigm that combined visual preference tasks adapted from pre-existing infant studies. OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study is to obtain developmental norms in six early social-emotional abilities in typical children aged 1 to 3 years that would be promising for an understanding of disorders of mental development. These developmental standards are essential to enable comparative assessments with children with atypical development, such as children with Profound Intellectual and Multiple Disabilities (PIMD). RESULTS: The participants had greater spontaneous visual preferences for biological (vs. non-biological) motion, socially salient (vs. non-social) stimuli, the eye (vs. mouth) area of emotional expressions, angry (vs. happy) faces, and objects of joint attention (vs. non-looked-at ones). Interestingly, although the prosocial (vs. antisocial) scene of the socio-moral task was preferred, both the helper and hinderer characters were equally gazed at. Finally, correlational analyses revealed that performance was neither related to participants' age nor to each other (dismissing the hypothesis of a common underpinning process). CONCLUSION: Our revised experimental paradigm is possible in infants aged 1 to 3 years and thus provides additional scientific proof on the direct assessment of these six socio-emotional abilities in this population.

abstract: Introduction As a key indicator of positive interpersonal interaction, interpersonal synchrony is widely considered to be closely related to individuals’ cooperative behavior. However, the mechanisms through which interpersonal synchrony influences cooperation in real classroom contexts remain insufficiently explored. Based on perceived similarity theory, social identity theory, and the psychological process model explaining how synchrony promotes cooperation, this study examines the impact of interpersonal synchrony on perceived cooperation among high school students and tests the mediating roles of perceived similarity and ingroup identification. Methods A combination of experimental manipulation and questionnaire measures was employed. A music-accompanied synchrony paradigm was used to manipulate interpersonal synchrony, while perceived similarity, ingroup identification, and perceived cooperation were measured. A multi-wave longitudinal design was adopted to analyze both the immediate effects of synchrony activities on perceived cooperation and the persistence of these effects over time. Results The results indicate that synchronous movement enhances perceived similarity, ingroup identification, and classroom perceived cooperation. Perceived similarity and ingroup identification play a chain mediating role between synchrony activities and perceived cooperation in high school psychology classes. Discussion Interpersonal synchrony not only improves students’ perceived cooperation in the classroom but also operates through psychological mechanisms involving perceived similarity and ingroup identification, thereby deepening the understanding of the social functions of synchrony.

abstract: Playful activities provide critical opportunities for rhythmic interactions, which may affect social and cognitive development in early childhood. Prior research suggests that motor synchrony promotes closeness and prosocial behaviour, but few studies have examined its role in social learning and in group settings. abstract: The gender stereotypes adults hold can influence whether they approve or disapprove of behavior shown by children, depending on whether this behavior is in line with stereotypes. Adults report negative evaluations toward children whose behavior does not adhere to gender stereotypes, particularly toward feminine boys. Whether pedagogical educators in training show negative reactions toward children who violate gender stereotypes has not been examined. We investigate this question by firstly assessing what gender stereotypes adults hold about children in Germany. In Study 1, we assessed descriptive, prescriptive, and proscriptive gender stereotypes identified by adults for children in German society. Stereotypes gathered from this first study were used to construct four vignettes of stereotypical and nonstereotypical boys and girls in order to examine how pedagogical educators in training (N = 414) evaluated these children in Study 2. We investigated ratings of one of these vignettes (2 × 2 between-participants design) regarding liking, perceived competence, creativity, self-esteem, prosocial behavior, as well as internalizing and externalizing problems. A series of ANOVAs revealed that girls displaying masculine behavior received advantageous ratings on competence, creativity, and self-esteem, while boys showing femininity were perceived as the most prosocial. More than gender nonconformity, masculinity and femininity strongly related to externalizing and internalizing problems, respectively. We review how our results in Germany differ from the literature originating in the USA, as we did not find backlash for feminine boys. Possible bias against femininity and toward masculinity within society and cultural and sampling factors is discussed.

abstract: School-aged children that experience social anxiety and have difficulty with interactions among peers can create significant challenges to their development in terms of both psychology and behavior. A team sport such as volleyball provides a common setting that naturally includes all aspects of social interaction (communication, cooperation, role coordination, etc.) and shared goals which is essential to improve the child's confidence in interacting socially and abilities to interact socially with peers. This research is an examination of the effect that a 12-week collective volleyball cooperative tactical training program will have on social anxiety and peer interaction in children (8-12). A sample of 80 healthy school-age children was obtained via two methods of campus based, voluntary and/or open recruitment. These children were then randomly assigned to either an experimental intervention group ( Group × Time Interaction Effects from a mixed-design ANOVA were found to be statistically significant for both of the outcomes (social anxiety and peer interaction) of this study. Children participating in an intervention that included an instructional program using the Collective Volleyball Cooperative Tactical Training Model showed significantly greater improvement than did those in the Control Condition in reducing their level of social anxiety as well as improving their peer interaction abilities over the course of the 12-weeks. Although we found a statistically-significant improvement in both children's social anxiety, and their peer interaction skills through a 12-week program, there is no data available for us to understand if those positive results will continue into the future because we did not assess children at later points in time. Thus, future researchers are encouraged to consider extended assessment periods as part of their study designs to determine how long such interventions have an impact. Secondly, as a feasibility study in a controlled environment showed promise for implementation of cooperative tactical volleyball programs, there may be barriers to successful implementation in regular school settings such as lack of facilities, class size and teacher workload. Future research is needed to examine how cooperative tactical volleyball programs can be adapted to encompass large groups of students and incorporated into routine physical education curriculum. Furthermore, although the intervention showed feasibility under controlled conditions, implementation in regular school settings may face practical challenges, including limited facilities, larger class sizes, and teacher workload. Future studies should examine how cooperative volleyball tactical training can be adapted for broader school-based implementation. Collective Volleyball Cooperative Tactical Training is an effective method for reducing social anxiety and improving the ability of school aged children to interact with peers. The program offers a viable, school-based model for integrating sport skills acquisition (training) and psychosocial growth through physical activity.

abstract: Introduction. Parental attitudes toward children's rights may shape how children participate in health care according to their age and developmental level. Evidence from pediatric outpatient settings in Türkiye is limited. Objective. To examine the relationships among the subdimensions of parental attitudes toward children's rights and identify those sharing variance with Self-Determination attitudes. Population and methods. Cross-sectional, descriptive-correlational study conducted in the pediatric outpatient clinic of a tertiary hospital, April-June 2026. Of 860 invited parents, 513 completed the questionnaire (59.7%). The Parental Attitudes Toward Children's Rights Scale was used (subdimensions: State Assurance and Support, Care and Protection, Self-Determination; Cronbach's alpha 0.811-0.867). Two-stage hierarchical regression was applied, with sociodemographic variables in Block 1 and the two remaining attitudinal subdimensions in Block 2. Because the variables entered in Block 2 and the outcome derive from the same instrument, the findings were interpreted as shared attitudinal variance rather than as independent prediction. Results. Care and Protection had the highest mean (4.45 ± 0.34), followed by State Assurance and Support (4.39 ± 0.36); Self-Determination was the lowest (3.97 ± 0.37). Block 1 contributed negligibly (R² = 0.011; p = 0.322). Block 2 substantially increased explained shared variance (R² = 0.523; ΔR² = 0.512; p < 0.001), with State Assurance and Support (β = 0.432) and Care and Protection (β = 0.332) both significant (p <0.001). Conclusions. Parents strongly endorsed protective and institutional-assurance rights, while self-determination scored lowest. These findings support addressing protective orientations together with the child's right to participate in pediatric care.

abstract: The development of moral reasoning and social behavior in adolescents and young adults is critical to healthy functioning. Sport participation is frequently assumed to promote positive developmental outcomes; however, the moral implications of participation in combative sports such as wrestling remain debated. Wrestling differs from many team and individual sports due to its physically dominant and one-on-one competitive structure, raising questions regarding how involvement may relate to moral identity, moral disengagement, and social behavior. The purpose of this exploratory quantitative study was to examine associations among moral identity, moral disengagement, and prosocial and antisocial behavior in adolescent and young adult athletes who participate exclusively in individual sports. Other variables of interest included years of participation in wrestling, gender, and sport type (combat or non-combat) whether they predicted variation in moral and behavioral constructs. Fifty-three participants included adolescent and young adult individual sport athletes between the ages of 12 and 22. Correlational and multivariate analyses were conducted to examine relationships among variables. Moral disengagement demonstrated a significant positive association with antisocial behavior in sport. Moral identity was not significantly related to antisocial behavior and showed only a small, non-significant association with prosocial behavior. Years of participation in wrestling and sport type did not significantly predict moral identity, moral disengagement, or social behavior. Gender differences emerged for moral disengagement and antisocial behavior, with female wrestlers reporting lower levels of both. These findings suggest that cognitive mechanisms used to justify behavior may play a more central role in antisocial conduct than moral self-concept alone. The results contribute to ongoing discussions regarding the developmental implications of participation in combat sports and provide groundwork for future research examining moral processes and behavior in individual sport contexts.

abstract: ABSTRACT Bystanders, organizational members who witness but are not directly involved in workplace bullying, are increasingly viewed as integral in addressing bullying. However, empirical evidence about how bystanders act and why is limited, having been hampered by the lack of a validated measure to capture bystander behavior. Drawing from previous typologies and extending a sensemaking model of bystanders, we theorize that there are four main classes of bystander behavior and that individual and organizational factors influence which of these is enacted when workplace bullying is witnessed. We develop the Bystander Typology Scale (BTS) to test our propositions, validating the new measure across three studies ( N Study 1a = 588; N Study 1b = 361; N Study 1c = 251), which show that the BTS captures four distinctive bystander behaviors: active constructive (e.g., confronting the perpetrator), passive constructive (e.g., offering emotional support), passive destructive (e.g., ignoring the situation), and active destructive (e.g., revictimization). Our main study ( N Study 2 = 374) shows that self‐efficacy, dark triad traits, and organizational conflict cultures influence bystander behavior in distinctive ways. Our research contributes to a greater understanding of how bystanders behave when witnessing bullying and why, alongside a tool for researchers to examine bullying bystanders systemically and for practitioners to evaluate interventions.

abstract: Ethical issues in anatomy have evolved over many years, driven by a medley of forces both internal and external to anatomy. Since the 1960s the focus of these developments has been on the centrality of informed consent of the donors and/or their families. This has made anatomists confront past unethical practices, even those that contributed in major ways to the establishment of anatomy as a research-based discipline. In tracing the emergence of anatomy as an ethically aware discipline, the ethical context alongside the scientific contributions of Vesalius and others has to be addressed. Over the years a gradually increasing appreciation of ethical boundaries has emerged, with significant ethical shifts occurring from the 1960s onwards, and marked in the United Kingdom by legislation commencing in 1961. Succeeding changes were characterized by increasing emphasis on the perspectives of patients and next of kin marked initially by the phrase "lack of objection," to be followed later by their fully informed consent. These developments were boosted by responses to the body parts scandals, leading to ethical values delineated in the 2004 Human Tissue Act. Ways of responding to varying perspectives of non-Western cultures, and their responses to informed consent are outlined. Plastination has burgeoned both publicly and educationally since the 1990s, introducing a plethora of ethical challenges for anatomists, due to the hybrid nature of plastinated material. Although the history of anatomy has been marked by compromise and pragmatism, consent has increasingly emerged as the ethical lynch pin.

abstract: Bullying is frequently used alongside prosocial strategies to achieve social dominance while minimizing social costs. However, the nature of this combination remains unclear, as prosocial strategies have been variously conceptualized as altruistic, mutually beneficial, or competitive and self-serving. The present study investigates whether bullying is associated with cooperative prosocial strategies—marked by collaboration, reciprocity, and mutual benefit—or with socially manipulative strategies characterized by ingratiation, insincerity, and manipulation for self-serving ends. A sample of 477 secondary school students (54.5% boys, 45.5% girls; Mage = 15.49) completed peer nomination measures assessing bullying, cooperative prosocial strategies and social manipulation, and three facets of social power: social dominance (dominance and popularity), peer affection (likeability and number of friendships), and dating popularity. Results indicated that bullying was significantly associated with socially manipulative strategies but not with cooperative strategies. Cooperative strategies were most strongly linked to cooperative relationships with an expectation of mutual benefit (peer affection, dating popularity), whereas social manipulation had the strongest association with social dominance, a more competitive form of social power. Boys’ direct bullying, and indirect bullying combined with high levels of social manipulation, were positively related to social dominance. These findings underscore the importance of distinguishing cooperative prosocial strategies from social manipulation and suggest that socially acceptable cooperative behaviors may serve as viable alternatives to bullying within anti-bullying interventions.

abstract: Gestational surrogacy has become an increasingly important pathway to parenthood for individuals and couples who cannot otherwise achieve or safely sustain pregnancy, yet its expansion has intensified longstanding ethical and regulatory controversy. Drawing on an extensive review of the literature summarized in Supplementary Table 1, this narrative review synthesizes contemporary ethical arguments and regulatory debates concerning gestational surrogacy. The analysis focuses on the tension between reproductive autonomy and concerns regarding exploitation, commodification, structural inequality, and the welfare of children. This synthesis identifies a growing challenge to the traditional binary distinction between commercial and altruistic surrogacy: payment alone does not determine whether an arrangement is exploitative, while altruistic models may also involve coercive pressures arising from familial obligations, social expectations, or economic dependence. At the same time, the child's interests, including secure legal parentage, citizenship, knowledge of origins, and recognition of the gestational relationship, have moved closer to the center of ethical analysis. Regulatory approaches remain highly heterogeneous, ranging from permissive commercial systems to altruistic-only models and complete prohibition. Against a broadly regulationist academic and professional literature, recent political initiatives, most notably the 2023 Casablanca Declaration and increasingly critical European parliamentary discourse, have strengthened an abolitionist framing of surrogacy as a threat to human dignity and a potential form of reproductive exploitation. We argue that the contemporary debate has therefore reached a moral crossroads: the central question is no longer simply whether surrogacy should be commercial or altruistic, but whether exploitation is intrinsic to gestational surrogacy or contingent on the conditions under which it is practiced. A coherent future framework should protect gestational carriers and children while respecting reproductive autonomy, and should address the transnational nature of surrogacy through stronger regulatory coordination.

abstract: Studying prosociality in rodents can provide insight into brain mechanisms potentially related to neurodevelopmental disorders known to impact social behaviors (e.g., autism spectrum disorder). While many studies have been published suggesting promising models, current knowledge remains scattered, including potential factors mediating prosocial behaviors in rodents. Prosocial behavior is characterized by an action done to benefit another or promote their well-being. The goal of this scoping review is to characterize current findings regarding prosocial paradigms in rodents, highlight current gaps in reporting, and identify factors shown to be important in mediating prosocial responses in rodents. Five databases were consulted in search of relevant studies published between 2000 and 2020 (APA PsycInfo, Embase, MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science). An update using a semi-supervised machine learning approach (ASReview) was then conducted to collect studies from 2021-2023. In total, 80 articles were included. Findings were the following: (1) Three categories of prosocial paradigm were extracted: cooperation, helping, and sharing tasks, (2) Rodents showed the ability to perform prosocial actions in all three categories, (3) Significant gaps in reported methodologies (e.g., failure to report animals' characteristics, housing conditions, and/or experimental protocol) and mediating factors (e.g., sex, strain, housing, food restriction) were found, and (4) Behaviors are determinant when investigating prosociality in rodents, however many studies omitted to include such analyses. Together these results inform future studies on the impact of mediating factors and the importance of behavioral analyses on the expression of prosocial behaviors in rodents.

abstract: Abstract The experimental literature in economics largely acknowledges the role of social capital in social payoff enhancing behavior and/or voluntary provision of public goods. However, social capital is often measured using different proxies that, in principle, may have different impacts on contributions. In this article, we unpack social capital in three dimensions (i.e., school, family, and friends) and we analyze which dimension matters for contributions in economic experiments. We collect data from an ultimatum game, a trust game, and a public good game carried out with children in primary and secondary schools in Sicily, Italy. To measure social capital, we also collect detailed information on social attitudes related to different contexts. We find that, as expected, social capital matters for contributions. More interestingly, we find that the only component that affects contributions is social capital at school. Our findings shed a light on how the school environment may be extremely important for the formation of social capital, especially when this is linked to behavior within the same environment.

abstract: Prior studies have investigated the relationship between fairness and honesty. However, the differences in the focus of these studies have rendered cross-comparisons between them challenging and of limited value. Thus, this study explored how fairness impacts honest decision-making, focusing specifically on the effect of individuals' experiences of fairness on their honest behavior. Experiment 1 explored the influence of different experiences of fairness on honest behavior in an altruistic context. In Experiment 2, we measured event-related potentials to further demonstrate the brain mechanisms of these experiences on altruistic dishonest behavior. In Experiment 1, we found that the reaction time for dishonest behavior was shorter for individuals who had positive unfairness experiences with high altruistic objects compared to low altruistic objects. Individuals who had negative unfairness experiences had shorter reaction times when engaging in dishonest behaviors for the sake of high altruistic objects compared to those with equitable experiences. In Experiment 2, in which there was an opportunity to lie for a highly altruistic object, those with fair experiences had greater N2 volatility and smaller P3 volatility than those with positive unfairness experiences. These findings highlight the value of integrating moral psychology and behavioral economics. Discriminant validity across fairness experiences can help illuminate the different motivations behind moral decisions.

abstract: This thesis explores the behavioural, contextual, and perceptual foundations of superficial charm, presenting a reconceptualisation of charm as a multidimensional, context-sensitive, and socially regulated construct. Across six empirical studies, it develops and tests the Superficial Charm Measure (SCM), which differentiates superficial charm into three core behavioural dimensions: Performed Social Fluency, Strategic and Instrumental, and Genuine Prosocial. These factors reflect distinct, but interacting, modes of charm expression, ranging from emotionally sincere and affiliative behaviours to those that are strategically motivated and manipulative. Using a multi-method approach—including qualitative thematic analysis, psychometric scale development, facial expression analysis, and interaction paradigms—this research examines how charm is broadcast, perceived, and interpreted across interpersonal contexts. Study 1 used qualitative interviews to identify behavioural traits associated with both charm and superficial charm, forming the foundation for item development. Studies 2 and 3 refined and tested the three-factor structure of the SCM. Studies 4 through 6 examined contextual moderators of charm perception, including social power, sex, observer bias, and the distinction between third-party observers and direct recipients. Key findings demonstrate that sex, social power, and target familiarity with the charmer significantly influence how charm is interpreted. The findings position superficial charm as a norm-driven, strategic, and co-constructed interpersonal behaviour. It is a measurable, socially embedded phenomenon that lies at the intersection of authenticity, influence and deception. Additionally, the development of the candidate measure, the SCM, contributes a novel tool to clinical, forensic, organisational, and interpersonal contexts, as well as the study of social influence, impression management, and social perception—although further validation is required.

abstract: Social media platforms increasingly serve as the primary place where people participate in public conversations about news. In these conversations, ad hominem attacks are quite common. Such ad hominem attacks might be influenced by underlying cognitive or affective goals, such as to discredit a purveyor of falsified evidence or to signal social distance from a hateful provocateur. They may also be driven by a simple operative goal: to stop what was said. When ad hominem attacks are used to stop the comments of another person, we refer to it as a discursive objection tactic. In this paper, we explore the prevalence of ad hominem attacks and characteristics of other discursive tactics used by people when objecting to online news commentary. First, we conducted a content analysis of more than 6,500 comment replies to trending news videos on YouTube and Twitter and identified seven distinct discursive objection tactics. Second, we examined the frequency of each tactic's occurrence from the 6,500 comment replies, as well as from a second sample of 2,004 replies. Our findings confirm that while ad hominem attacks are the most common discursive tactic used to object to news commentary, people also deploy a diversity of other discursive objection tactics. The resulting typology offers a comprehensive account of grassroots efforts which utilize deterrent speech, nonaccommodative communication and prosocial strategies.

abstract: Creative thinking emerges as a critical skill that adds meaning to individuals' lives in today's competitive world. One of the learning environments aimed at developing this skill is the Discovery Campus, which serves as a children's university. This qualitative study aimed to investigate the perceptions and experiences regarding creative thinking of 32 children aged 11-13 who regularly attend the Discovery Campus in Gaziantep, Türkiye. The participants were selected through criterion sampling, a purposive sampling method. Data were collected via written interview forms and analysed using the content analysis method. The findings indicated that participants perceive the Discovery Campus as a learning environment where, in addition to acquiring new knowledge, they can apply what they have learned, discover their own potential, and develop original ideas. It was determined that creative project ideas aim to develop solutions to problems based on the needs of humans, society, and living organisms; and that experiences at the Discovery Campus are associated with an approach based on hands-on learning, material use, enquiry, observation, and imagination, which differs from formal school environments. Furthermore, in the children's narratives, it was observed that opportunities for creative thinking are shaped by the processes of conducting research, focusing on areas of interest, participating in workshop activities, transforming ideas into projects, and sharing the developed designs. Accordingly, in order to support children's creative thinking processes, it is recommended to expand science centres that bring together different disciplines and provide opportunities for practical application and project production.

abstract: Networked problem solving underlies the formative dynamics of a variety of complex systems. In this setting it is important to consider not just what network ties exist, but how ties change over time, and the influence this has on the behavior and exchange facilitated by these interactions. Ranging from cellular communication to human organization, collectives engage in goal-oriented behavior and adapt to maximize their rewards. When considering a network tie between two problem solvers, optimal group-level outcomes often depend on two overarching concepts: cooperation and coordination. The first two projects of this dissertation use stylized models of networked problem solvers to demonstrate how preferential interaction (i.e., adapting network ties to maximize individual rewards) can lead to distinct system dynamics. In one setting, preferential interaction is shown to harm cooperative prosocial behaviors, while in the other it promotes coordination and robustness. The first agent-based model demonstrates the conditions under which spiteful behavior could emerge. Spite is a behavior that harms both the actor and recipient, and therefore its emergence is evolutionarily counterintuitive. The model demonstrates that if agents are able to interact preferentially, spiteful behavior can gain a relative advantage and become the norm in a population. A second agent-based model examines the formation of signaling conventions under preferential interaction. This is the first model to demonstrate agents' use of a novel form of signaling, where communicating partners failed to reach a consensus on the meaning of each signal. Instead, agents solved the signaling problem by using the network structure to ensure two distinct types of complementary signaling strategies interacted. Finally, the third project reports on an online survey and experiment conducted on an online labor market platform. This project examines the psychological willingness of freelancers to cooperate in temporary teams, and how our results can inform platform design aimed at strengthening the social ties between freelancers. Our results suggest that our freelance participants display traits that are more consistent with belonging to a shared, coherent group than would be expected given existing theory. Overall, the chapters of this dissertation consider self-organization in game theoretic and real-world settings, and show how emergent behaviors are influenced type of relational links that form. --Author's abstract

abstract: Altruistic cooperation (AC) is essential in human social interactions. Previous studies have investigated AC-related behavior in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), revealing that there is considerable individual variability in the behavior. However, this issue is still largely unexplored especially in the adult population. To investigate individual differences in AC-related behavior, we conducted the resource allocation task (RAT) and modified version of the ultimatum game (mUG) among adults with and without ASD. The study employed a cross-sectional design, involving 27 adults with ASD (mean age 29.1 ± 4.3 years; three females) and 27 adults with typical development (TD) (mean age 25.8 ± 6.7 years; two females), who completed the RAT and mUG tasks. Beyond clinical characteristics, we assessed three primary psychological metrics: the interpersonal reactivity index (IRI), Barratt impulsiveness scale, and the behavioral inhibition and activation systems. No significant differences were observed in the proportions of participants with high AC when assessed by RAT (p = 0.15) and mUG (p = 0.59) between the TD and ASD groups. Participants with high AC from the RAT demonstrated higher perspective-taking scores on the IRI than those with low AC within both the TD (p = 0.04) and ASD groups (p = 0.03). In the TD group, high AC individuals also scored higher on the IRI's fantasy subscale as per the mUG (p = 0.03); however, this trend was not present in the ASD group. The present findings indicate that empathy plays an important role in individual differences in AC-related behavior among adults with and without ASD, although the role could be different depending on the types of AC-related behavior between TD and ASD populations.

abstract: Problematic short-form video use (PSVU) has emerged as a pressing public health issue. Although research on this topic is expanding, few studies have systematically explored the complex predictors of problematic short-form video use across genders. This study sought to combine network analysis and machine learning (ML) to decode the associations between social bonds and problematic short-form video use across genders. A cross-sectional survey of 2076 Chinese adolescents (51.73% girls, mean age = 13.75) assessed problematic short-form video use, social bonds (attachment, commitment, involvement, belief), and demographic information. Results indicated that PSVU2 (i.e., increasing time for satisfaction) was the central symptom of problematic short-form video use across genders. ML findings revealed that commitment was the most predictive dimension for the central symptom of problematic short-form video use in both boys and girls, followed by belief, involvement, attachment, and demographic information at the dimension level. At the factor level, the top six factors with the greatest predictive contributions in girls were academic engagement, prosocial behaviors, mindfulness, responsibility, belief in a just world, and grit. In boys, these factors were responsibility, academic engagement, mindfulness, grit, parent-child relationships, and belief in a just world. These findings offer both theoretical insights and practical guidance for intervention strategies targeting adolescent problematic short-form video use.

abstract: OBJECTIVES: To examine the effects of price transparency and prosocial messaging on price-protected consumers' health care choices as a potential cost-saving strategy to manage rising US health care expenditures. STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional study. Participants were recruited to complete a basic questionnaire via Amazon's Mechanical Turk program. Participants' selections were subsequently collected and analyzed. METHODS: Participants (N = 567) selected a sleep study provider from 5 options, with manipulations including financial responsibility, provision of price information, and a prosocial message encouraging high-value options. RESULTS: Price transparency increased the selection of lower-cost options among participants who were solely responsible for paying for their own health care expenses. For participants whose insurance paid for health care expenses, both price transparency and prosocial messaging were necessary to choose lower-cost options. CONCLUSIONS: The study highlights the importance of considering both financial and social factors in patient engagement initiatives, suggesting that a combination of price transparency and prosocial messaging can influence health care choices and potentially contribute to cost-saving strategies in the US health care system.

abstract: Palliative care has matured as a life-span field with an increasing research base. Advancing the field means understanding why patients and caregivers participate in palliative care research, and participation's benefits and burdens. This study extended previous work to include greater diversity of clinical sampling and study design. Prospective, multi-methods study examined reported benefits, burdens, and motivations associated with participation in pediatric palliative care research. Study pParticipants included patients, caregivers, and family members who enrolled in pediatric palliative care research, as well as individuals declining participation, within a single quaternary pediatric hospital system. Structured questionnaires were administered at enrollment and study completion; qualitative responses were analyzed thematically. 57 participants completed the questionnaires. Altruism and personal benefit were the most frequently cited motivations for enrollment at baseline and study completion. Emotional expression and the opportunity to help others were commonly identified as positive aspects of participation. The majority reported no discomfort and indicated willingness to participate in future research. The most frequent reasons given for declining participation were feeling overwhelmed, lack of interest, or study-specific aversion, rather than distress associated with palliative care research iPPC involvement. Participants consistently reported greater benefit than burden, suggesting that pediatric palliative care research participation is acceptable and often meaningful. Given the pre/post design, the findings suggest eligible participants are able to determine if actual study participation is likely beneficial for them or not. Supporting families as they consider research participation promotes ethical, sensitive, and inclusive research design. Identified patterns may guide research design for future investigators to continue to advance the science of pediatric palliative care across the lifespanresearch.

abstract: Abstract Do young infants expect people to help one another? In two experiments (N = 72), the present study examined 5.5-month-old infants’ helping expectations as they watched two female agents’ actions. After seeing one agent try but fail to obtain an out-of-reach toy and then exit, infants expected another agent to help by moving the toy within her reach and found it unexpected when the agent did not. Importantly, if the first agent did not try to reach for the toy, signaling no need for it, infants instead found it unexpected when the other agent helped. Together, these results suggest that infants at this young age already expect people to be helpful toward others in need. These findings thus shed new light on the early development of moral cognition.

abstract: This study explores healthcare quality from the viewpoints of patients and parents during daily interactions with healthcare professionals in pediatric care. A focused ethnography was conducted at a Dutch children's hospital. Nine patients were observed and eight in-depth interviews were conducted with parents and, when possible, patients. Data was refined through discussions with a diverse research team, including two patients, and the hospital's parent advisory board. Eleven categories were identified, such as genuine contact, dealing with emotions, and sharing responsibility for care. These were clustered into five themes to highlight broader patterns: (1) Feeling prepared, (2) Feeling truly seen, (3) Attentive, reciprocal relationship, (4) Calmness, and (5) Space for feelings. Meaningful pediatric care was experienced in small, everyday moments in which patients and parents felt recognized, prepared, safe, calm, and supported. These findings underscore the importance of emphasizing interpersonal aspects of care in everyday clinical interactions.

abstract: Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) is the standard of care treatment for Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome (OSAS) in children with Down Syndrome (DS). Implementation and adherence can be difficult. The aim of this study was to conduct a qualitative exploration of parental experiences of NIV. Semi-structured interviews were completed with 18 parents of children with DS and OSAS treated with NIV. Reflexive Thematic Analysis was utilised. Parents' narratives reflected a journey characterised as "a rollercoaster of ups and downs." Five themes were generated from the interviews including: being intrinsically motivated, sharing the burden, maintaining hope while grappling with the challenges, taking account of the developmental context and finding balance. Unique insights underscored the dynamic role parents play in managing NIV amidst the complexities of their daily lives. The findings highlight the dynamic role parents play in managing NIV alongside the emotional, relational, and practical demands of daily life. By providing insight into both the challenges and adaptations involved, the study may help inform family-centred approaches to supporting children with Down syndrome undergoing NIV.

abstract: A popular topic in developmental science is self-regulation, an aspect of functioning viewed as contributing to optimal development. Of particular theoretical importance is top-down (frontal cortically based) self-regulation (TDSR). This article briefly reviews recent research on TDSR's relation to four areas of development: maladjustment, social competence, prosocial development, and academic development. Recent studies on the topic often involve sophisticated methods and designs; moreover, several relevant meta-analyses have been published in the recent past. In general, a higher level of TDSR has been associated with better adjustment, social competence, prosociality, and success in the school setting. Limitations in the research and extant meta-analyses are briefly noted.

abstract: Human cooperation unfolds in social environments where individuals influence each other through payoff-based learning and social comparison, the tendency to evaluate fitness relative to others. However, it is still unclear how social comparison and population structure jointly shape cooperation. Here, we incorporate social comparison theory into evolutionary dynamics on structured populations, letting fitness depend on individual and neighbour payoffs weighted by a comparison parameter. Under weak selection, we derive conditions favoring cooperation and find that the proposed comparison nonlinearly reshapes the critical benefit-to-cost ratio. Even one individual applying this protocol can affect the population, especially in heterogeneous networks. When comparison tendencies vary, the full distribution, not just the mean, determines evolutionary outcomes. Using a swarm-intelligence-based framework across typical and empirical networks, we identify cooperation-maximizing patterns: optimal states exhibit heterogeneous comparison tendencies, yet collectively align toward assimilative development. These results provide a basis for designing social incentives that harness comparison to promote collective cooperation in human groups.

abstract: This article delves into charitable behavior through the lens of economics, exploring how altruism and generosity intersect with economic decision-making. It traces the historical evolution of charity, from its early roots in religious and ethical traditions in ancient civilizations, such as Egypt and Greece, to its institutionalization in modern philanthropic practices during the Industrial Revolution. The analysis draws heavily on behavioral economics, focusing on key theories like warm glow-giving, reciprocal altruism, and social preferences, which challenge traditional economic models of rational self-interest. abstract: Based on developmental systems and dynamic systems theories, we propose the lifeworld approach-a conceptual framework for research and a hypothesis concerning early social-cognitive development. As a framework, the lifeworld approach recognizes the social embeddedness of development and shifts the focus away from individual developmental outcomes toward the reciprocal interplay of processes within and between individuals that co-constitutes early social-cognitive development. As a hypothesis, the lifeworld approach proposes that the changing developmental system-spanning the different individuals as their subsystems-strives toward attractor states through regulation at the behavioral level, which results in both the emergence and further differentiation of developmental attainments. The lifeworld approach-as a framework and a hypothesis, including key methodological approaches to test it-is exemplified by research on infants' self-awareness, prosocial behavior and social learning. Equipped with, first, a conceptual framework grounded in a modern view on development and, second, a growing suite of methodological approaches, developmental science can advance by analyzing the mutually influential relations between intra-individual and interactional processes in order to identify key mechanisms underlying early social-cognitive development.

abstract: Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) face significant challenges in Theory of Mind (ToM), particularly in understanding others' perspectives. While serious games have shown potential, most existing interventions focus on basic emotion recognition without engaging narrative contexts. Objective: This pilot study aims to design a history-based serious game, "Tarumanegara Adventure," and evaluate its preliminary effectiveness in improving cognitive empathy among children with high-functioning ASD. Using a mixed-methods case study approach with a one-group pretest - post-test design, six students with ASD (aged 8-15) participated in a 2-week intervention. The game integrates historical narratives as a logical scaffold with explicit emotion scaffolding and moral decision-making mechanics. Data were analyzed using the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test and triangulated with behavioral observations. Quantitative results showed a significant increase in cognitive empathy scores (p = 0.0312) with a large effect size (Cohen’s d = 3.19). However, triangulation revealed a "knowing-doing gap," in which higher cognitive scores did not correlate significantly with spontaneous prosocial behavior (ρ = -0.36). Conclusion: The history-based narrative approach effectively enhances cognitive knowledge of empathy by providing a structured context. However, bridging the gap between cognitive understanding and spontaneous behavioral application remains a critical challenge for future game design.

abstract: Television viewing is a common feature of early childhood, including toddlerhood; however, evidence regarding the developmental implications of different types of television content in toddlerhood remains limited. The present study examined television viewing in two-year-old children across seven content dimensions, including pace, prosocial content, antisocial and aggressive content, educational strategies, depictions of emotions, mental state talk, and cultural consciousness. Findings highlight the importance of considering both quantity and quality when evaluating the impacts of early childhood media use.

abstract: The present study explored the psychosocial factors influencing blood donation behaviour among younger-age adults classified as non-donors in the United Kingdom. Six participants (aged 18–35) with no history of blood donation were recruited via opportunity sampling. Semi-structured interviews were conducted and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis to identify key patterns in participant narratives related to donation behaviour. Two overarching themes were identified. Barriers to blood donation included four sub-themes: (i) socially constructed misconceptions of eligibility and need, (ii) embodied discomfort and perceived invasiveness of the donation process, (iii) disengagement and deferred responsibility in blood donation, and (iv) perceived absence and inaccessibility of blood donation campaigns. Tailored public health strategies must address adult non-donors’ psychological and informational barriers, including misconceptions, procedural uncertainty, and anxiety about physical reactions. Interventions should pair targeted communication with accessible, accurate information and frame donation as both socially beneficial and personally rewarding.

abstract: Coordination problems are central to social and economic life and often involve multiple equilibria. Classical theories identify two canonical principles for equilibrium selection: maximizing payoffs and minimizing strategic risk. These principles differ in what they demand of a decision-maker: payoff-based coordination can be reached by recognizing that one equilibrium pays more, whereas risk-based coordination requires reasoning about what happens when coordination fails. Yet little is known about how the use of these principles varies from late childhood to early adulthood. Using a large sample of more than 2,000 participants aged 10 to 20, who played two coordination games and then stated the reason for each choice, we construct measures that pair each choice with a congruent stated reason and document an asymmetry in their age profiles. Payoff-based coordination is already high at the earliest ages studied and shows at most a weak age gradient. In contrast, risk-based coordination shows a modest but consistent increase with age. The difference between the two age gradients is statistically significant; the risk-based gradient also appears within the study using a common protocol across ages and in the risk-dominant choice itself. Cognitive ability shifts the level of both measures but does not alter their age profiles. These findings show that payoff-based and risk-based coordination vary differently with age, while similar observed choices can be accompanied by different stated reasons.

abstract: As large language models (LLMs) continue to gain popularity due to their human-like traits and the intimacy they offer to users, their societal impact inevitably expands. This leads to the rising necessity for comprehensive studies to fully understand LLMs and reveal their potential opportunities, drawbacks and overall societal impact. With that in mind, this research conducted an extensive investigation into seven LLMs, aiming to assess the temporal stability and inter-rater agreement on their responses on personality instruments in two time points. abstract: As clinical trials become more complex and distributed, principal investigators (PIs) face an expanding scope of oversight. ICH E6(R3) Good Clinical Practice permits delegation while retaining investigator responsibility and proportionate oversight for activities undertaken under their responsibility. Operational authority and portfolio-level oversight capacity often do not expand in proportion to these demands. This Perspective proposes a dual-mismatch framework: site-level clinical accountability may exceed both the PI's influence over operational dependencies and the capacity available to oversee them. The concern is not merely workload, but its relationship to authority and capacity. Decentralisation amplifies rather than creates these longstanding mismatches, although its net effect depends on how work is organised. Current regulatory provisions recognise relevant responsibilities but may not fully resolve these mismatches in practice. Four complementary directions are proposed: weighted portfolio-level capacity assessment, interface-level accountability mapping, operational levers, and redesigned distributed clinical leadership. These approaches preserve the PI's ultimate oversight responsibility while clarifying other parties' duties and sharing supervisory activities. The framework and proposed measures require empirical validation. A research agenda would examine their associations with timely safety review, important protocol deviations and data quality, and evaluate whether organisational changes improve oversight.

abstract: Perioperative care is a highly resource-intensive component of healthcare, with operating theatres consuming substantial energy and generating considerable waste and emissions. Sustainable perioperative practice is therefore essential to reduce environmental impact. However, there is limited understanding of how competencies in sustainable practice can be developed within operating theatre nursing education. In particular, little attention has been given to how educational interventions shape students’ professional agency in relation to sustainability. Collaborative Online International Learning (COIL) offers a pedagogical approach that supports reflective and intercultural learning and may offer opportunities to foster professional agency for sustainability. This protocol describes a mixed-methods, randomised, feasibility pilot study that aims to assess the feasibility and acceptability of implementing and evaluating two learning formats in international collaborative learning in theatre nursing education, while also generating preliminary insights into how these formats may influence students’ reflective work and expressions of professional agency. A 90-minute synchronous online seminar focusing on sustainable theatre nursing practice across perioperative care phases will be delivered as part of the curriculum to operating theatre nursing students at Karolinska Institutet (Sweden) and Oslo Metropolitan University (Norway). Students will be randomly allocated (1:1) to one of two formats: (1) phase-specific COIL, in which small groups focus on a single perioperative phase, followed by whole-group sharing across phases, with documentation in a digital space; or (2) cross-phase COIL, in which small groups address all phases, document their work using a self-selected format and subsequently engage in whole-group comparison. A pragmatic sample of 24–36 students is anticipated. Primary outcomes are feasibility and acceptability indicators, including consent rates, questionnaire completion and follow-up rates, intervention fidelity, participant engagement and the feasibility of repeated questionnaire administration. Qualitative data, including collaborative outputs and observer field notes, will be analysed using reflexive thematic analysis informed by a conceptual model of professional agency and sustainability competence. Comparative analyses will explore differences in the complexity of students’ expressions of professional agency across learning formats. Quantitative data will include students’ perceptions of intercultural collaboration and learning, as well as attitudes towards sustainability in the operating theatre, assessed before the seminar and 1 week later. Because questionnaire responses are anonymous and cannot be linked at the individual level, baseline and follow-up data will be analysed as independent aggregate datasets. Quantitative findings will therefore be interpreted descriptively and will not be used to assess individual-level changes over time. Integration of qualitative and quantitative findings will be conducted at the interpretation stage using a triangulation approach. The study has been approved by the Norwegian Agency for Shared Services in Education and Research (reference number 266740). In Sweden, the study was reviewed by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority (reference number 2026-00252-01), which concluded that the study did not require formal ethical approval under the Swedish Ethical Review Act and issued an advisory opinion. Participation in the research component is voluntary, and informed consent will be obtained. All data will be de-identified prior to analysis. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and conference presentations and will inform the design of a future randomised controlled trial (RCT) of an educational intervention aimed at supporting sustainable practice in operating theatre nursing education. abstract: Abstract Evolved nests are species-specific developmental systems that support biological, psychological, and social needs. The human evolved nest includes practices such as responsive care, self-directed play, and extensive affectionate touch. Previous studies have linked childhood experience of these practices to both child and adult well-being. Here we assessed whether recall of evolved nest experiences during childhood (age 0–18) was related to three dimensions of adult well-being and social capital (personal well-being, social relationships, and general prosociality) in three countries (USA, UK, Japan). Recalled evolved nest experience was positively associated with multiple measures under each dimension across cultures after controlling for demographic factors ( n = 1,401). In contrast, it was not found to be associated with incentivised measures of prosociality (elicited via a series of economic games) in any country. Exploratory factor analyses revealed that experiences of evolved nest practices clustered together under two common factors in each country: positive and negative experiences. These factors were independently associated with multiple indicators of adult well-being and social capital in each country, and these associations were generally stronger for positive (vs. negative) experiences. Our findings are consistent with the hypothesis that childhood experience of the evolved nest has long-term benefits for individual and societal well-being regardless of cultural differences.

abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Social and Emotional Education (SEE) interventions during early childhood have shown considerable promise in enhancing children's emotion understanding, social competence, and behavioural adjustments. However, few studies have examined their long-term impact, especially across the preschool-to-primary school transition. This study evaluated the effectiveness of a manualized SEE program, Timmy's Trip to Planet Earth, in promoting emotional, behavioural, and social functioning over time. METHODS: = 44). The program combined teacher training, classroom-based lessons, home activities, and teachers' ongoing implementation support. The effectiveness of the program was measured via the Test of Emotion Comprehension (TEC), the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ), and the Social Competence and Behavior Evaluation (SCBE-30). RESULTS: Significant Time × Group interactions were observed for the TEC External and Mental components, indicating greater improvements in emotion recognition and mental state understanding in the intervention group. The SDQ revealed significant reductions in conduct problems and increased prosocial behaviours. In the SCBE-30, a significant interaction effect was found for social competence, with the intervention group showing greater improvement over time compared to the control group. CONCLUSIONS: The findings suggest that SEE programs can produce meaningful and lasting improvements in children's emotional and social skills across key educational transitions. Teacher training and family involvement likely played a critical role in supporting the program's sustained impact.

abstract: In this study, we examine how changes in monetary incentives offered to online consultants on e-consultation platforms shape the direction of their free knowledge contributions across specialized and non-specialized domains. We use the sudden suspension and subsequent resumption of the Fenda platform as two exogenous shocks to the monetary incentives these online consultants receive, and implement a difference-in-differences estimation. Our study shows that monetary incentives shift the direction of online consultants’ free knowledge contributions. Rather than delving deeper into their specialized domains and engaging with even unpopular topics, they tend to broaden their contributions across a broader array of non-specialized domains. The findings enrich the literature on knowledge management and provide valuable guidance for managers of e-consultation platforms.

abstract: Commissioning and funding agencies have an increasing role in translating and implementing national policies to improve primary care access, whilst being sensitive to the needs of local contexts. Integrated Care Boards (ICBs) are meso-level commissioning organisations that sit in between national bodies and general practices in the National Health Service (NHS) in England. In this study we examine the role of ICBs in facilitating improvements in access to general practice. Qualitative rapid evaluation in three English NHS districts (ICB areas) focused on the role of the ICB in supporting access-focused improvements to primary care services. The study included semi-structured interviews ( ICBs were found to perform three key roles in facilitating and implementing access-related quality improvement: 1) translational work to contextualise national funding priorities and objectives to the local level; 2) relational work to build trustbased relationships with practices and system stakeholders including local government, at-scale primary care providers, and patient groups; and 3) developmental work to establish infrastructure to support quality improvement, including knowledge-sharing and data analytics capacity. Commissioners play a critical role in bridging national and local contexts to support quality improvement in primary care. The capacity and capability of ICBs to carry out this role are however limited by ongoing organisational restructuring initiated by national policy makers and by constrained resources.

abstract: A recent philanthropic movement with advocates among high-profile tech entrepreneurs and philosophers, effective altruism (EA) has been widely disparaged for its flawed moral philosophy and conservative political implications. As philanthropic practice, however, it has been seldom studied. In this paper, we argue that claims to technoscientific expertise are central to how EA actors understand, legitimize, and take part in the production of philanthropic value. We analyze their practices of categorization, ranking and measurement as well as underlying technoscientific imaginaries and moral views through comparing three areas of EA intervention: neglected tropical diseases, cultured meat, and AI safety. We show how EA involves various and contested ambitions to direct knowledge production and redraw the boundaries of expert communities, shedding light on the centrality of technoscience in philanthropists' worldmaking ambitions.

abstract: Children's social behavior develops through diverse experiences. However, the relationship between children's experiences of celebratory events and their behavioral development has not been previously quantified. Therefore, this study aimed to quantitatively explore this relationship. In 2020, a self-reported questionnaire was completed by 653 sixth-grade students (aged 11-12 years) and/or their caregivers in Nagoya, Aichi, a major metropolitan area in Japan. The main items surveyed were children's experiences with events celebrated by their family and their behavioral development. The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire was used to assess children's behavior. This questionnaire identifies behavioral and emotional problems and prosocial behavior. Multiple regression analysis was conducted with the number of family events experienced by children as the explanatory variable and their emotional and prosocial behavior as the objective variables. Children from families who participated in fewer family events tended to have higher problematic behavior risk scores and lower prosociality scores compared with their counterparts. Compared with children who participated in more than 20 family events, those who participated in fewer than 10 family events had more than three times the risk for exhibiting problem behaviors (odds: 3.558, 95% CI: 1.252-10.111, p = .017) and prosocial problems (odds: 3.184, 95% CI: 1.726-5.876, p < .001). Conversely, children from families who participated in more family events tended to have lower problematic behavior risk scores and higher prosociality scores. A higher number of family events may reduce the risk of behavioral problems in children and increase their prosociality. Enjoying family events may be beneficial for social adjustment.

abstract: Background: Donor human milk (DHM) is a critical alternative for vulnerable infants when maternal milk is unavailable, but its clinical utilisation in South Africa is constrained by limited understanding of how maternal knowledge, perceived safety, cultural meanings and social contexts shape local acceptance. Aim: To explore postnatal mothers' knowledge, perceptions and sociocultural influences shaping acceptance of DHM in Richards Bay, KwaZulu-Natal. Methods: A qualitative design informed by interpretive phenomenology was used. Twenty-two postnatal mothers were purposively recruited from a private hospital. Semi-structured interviews were conducted in English or isiZulu, and data were transcribed, translated where necessary, and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis supported by reflexivity, peer debriefing, member checking and an audit trail. Results: Four themes were developed. DHM was largely unfamiliar, with participants reporting limited prior information and little exposure through routine maternal healthcare. Safety concerns centred on infection, donor health, screening, storage and milk processing, although confidence in healthcare institutions facilitated acceptance for some mothers. Acceptance was also shaped by maternal identity, emotional attachment to breastfeeding, spiritual and cultural beliefs, and family and community influence. Limited awareness did not equate to fixed rejection: after DHM was explained, participants distinguished between receiving and donating: willingness to receive DHM for their own infants was conditional on safety assurance and provider recommendation, whereas willingness to donate was expressed more readily and was often motivated by altruism and reciprocity. These findings indicate an interaction between informational uncertainty, institutional trust, cultural meaning and social legitimacy in shaping DHM decisions. Conclusion: Supporting informed decision-making about DHM, and potentially its uptake, requires more than increasing awareness. Routine antenatal and postnatal education, provider training, transparent communication about safety, and culturally responsive family and community engagement may help convert conditional openness into informed acceptance and donation.

abstract: ABSTRACT In response to concerns regarding how disaster relief nonprofit organizations distribute financial donations, this paper explores individual donor giving, intent upon giving, and expectations subsequent to giving, in the context of the 2019/20 Kangaroo Island bushfires in South Australia. Adopting fundamental constructs from the theory of planned behavior, we examine why people give to natural disaster fundraising campaigns. We then compare donor intent and their expectations of nonprofits subsequent to giving, with nonprofits' actions and communication to consider how (un/met) expectations might impact on attitudes to future giving. A qualitative approach was adopted involving 14 semi‐structured interviews with individual donors (most of whom were geographically close to the disaster location), publicly available communication regarding the disaster, and e‐mail correspondence with the relevant nonprofits. Findings reveal the importance of closeness (geographical, emotional and psychological) to a range of factors influencing giving behavior. Contrary to extant literature that cautions a misalignment between donors' intent, expectations, and nonprofits' actions, this occurrence did not impact negatively on donors' satisfaction or attitudes towards future giving behavior. Implications extend to better understanding why donors give, their expectations following a natural disaster, and the multiple dimensions of donor closeness.
